title: Sexual and reproductive health and contraception
blurb: Advise on when fertility returns, which methods can start straight after birth, when combined methods are safe, and when breastfeeding counts as contraception.
question: Chloe is on the postnatal ward, 2 days after the birth of her second baby. She is breastfeeding and wants to restart the combined pill she used before pregnancy. What should the midwife advise?

teach.h: Fertility returns sooner than women expect
teach.body: A woman can become pregnant from 3 weeks after giving birth, even if she is breastfeeding and her periods have not returned. Waiting at least 12 months before the next pregnancy is usually advised, as conceiving sooner may raise risks such as low birth weight. So SPM 3.4 asks midwives to give women information about, and access to, sexual and reproductive health services, including contraception, before they leave maternity care.
teach.cite: NHS: Sex and contraception after birth (reviewed Feb 2024); NICE NG194 1.2.1; SPM 3.4

items.label: Implant, injection, POP, condoms: any time
IUD or IUS can be fitted

IUD or IUS if missed the 48 h window

teach.caption: Feeding less often or longer gaps between feeds also end LAM. Expressing may make it less effective.

teach.body: Sexual and reproductive health includes sex after birth, sexually transmitted infections and the woman's rights over her own fertility. There are no rules about when to resume sex; lubricant helps with dryness, and pain that persists at the postnatal check should be raised with the GP. A new partner or STI concern is a reason to offer sexual health services and, during pregnancy, repeat IDPS testing.

Chloe is breastfeeding, so the combined pill should usually wait until at least 6 weeks. Fertility can return from 3 weeks, so she needs cover before then. The midwife explains the options she can start straight away, including the progestogen-only pill, implant or injection, and mentions that an IUD or IUS could be fitted within 48 hours or from 4 weeks. Chloe chooses the POP; the plan is recorded and passed to her GP and health visitor.

teach.text: 'Breastfeeding is natural contraception' is true ONLY while all three LAM conditions hold. A single bottle of formula, a dummy, solids, any bleeding or the baby passing 6 months ends it. And an IUD missed in the first 48 hours waits until 4 weeks, not 6.

items.label: window for IUD or IUS after birth

items: Pregnancy is possible from 3 weeks after birth, breastfeeding or not.
Implant, injection, POP and condoms can start straight after birth, including when breastfeeding.
IUD or IUS within 48 hours of birth, otherwise from 4 weeks.
Combined pill, ring or patch: from 3 weeks if not breastfeeding and no VTE risk; usually from 6 weeks if breastfeeding.
LAM needs breast milk only, a baby under 6 months and no periods.
Offer information and access to sexual health services; aim for at least 12 months before the next pregnancy.

summary: You can now tell a woman when her fertility returns, which methods she can start immediately, when combined methods are safe with and without breastfeeding, and whether LAM applies. You can also signpost her to sexual and reproductive health services.

A.q: A woman asks how soon after the birth she could become pregnant again if she is breastfeeding and has had no period. What is the correct answer?
A.why: NHS guidance: a woman can get pregnant from 3 weeks after birth, including if she is breastfeeding and her periods have not returned.

whyNot.0: Six weeks is later than fertility can return.
whyNot.2: Twelve weeks greatly overestimates the safe period.
whyNot.3: Ovulation comes before the first period, so she can conceive before it.

A.q: An IUS was not fitted within 48 hours of birth. From when can it usually be fitted?
A.why: NHS: if an IUD or IUS is not fitted within 48 hours of birth, wait until 4 weeks after the birth.

whyNot.0: Two weeks is inside the period when fitting is not advised.
whyNot.1: There is no need to wait until 12 weeks.
whyNot.3: Timing is set by weeks since birth, not periods.

A.q: Which method can a breastfeeding woman start straight after giving birth?
A.why: The POP, implant, injection, condoms and IUD/IUS (within 48 hours) can all be started straight after birth, including when breastfeeding.

whyNot.0: The combined pill usually waits until at least 6 weeks when breastfeeding.
whyNot.1: The ring is a combined method, usually from 6 weeks if breastfeeding.
whyNot.2: The patch is a combined method, usually from 6 weeks if breastfeeding.

B.q: Priya is formula feeding and has no risk factors for a blood clot. From when can she start the combined pill?
B.why: NHS: if not breastfeeding and checked for VTE risk factors, combined pill, ring or patch can start 3 weeks after the birth.

whyNot.1: Combined methods are not started immediately because of postnatal clot risk.
whyNot.2: Six weeks is the usual start when breastfeeding.
whyNot.3: Waiting 12 weeks leaves her unprotected after fertility returns.

B.q: Kemi's baby is 4 months old and exclusively breastfed, and she has had no periods. She has just started one bottle of formula at night. What should the midwife or health visitor advise?
options: Continue LAM until the baby is 6 months old
LAM still works if most feeds are breast
Use LAM until her periods come back
Start another method, as LAM no longer applies
B.why: LAM requires breast milk only; giving formula, a dummy or solids means another form of contraception is needed (NHS).

whyNot.0: The 6-month limit applies only while all three conditions are met.
whyNot.1: Any formula ends LAM, however many breastfeeds there are.
whyNot.2: Periods are one end point, but formula has already ended LAM.

B.q: A woman asks how long she should wait before trying for another baby. What interval is usually advised?
B.why: NHS: it is usually recommended to wait at least 12 months after giving birth, as a shorter gap may increase risks such as low birth weight.

whyNot.0: Three months is shorter than the advised gap.
whyNot.1: Six months is shorter than the advised gap.
whyNot.3: A minimum gap of 12 months is advised.

C.q: Chloe, day 2 postnatal, is mixed feeding her baby. She wants to restart the combined pill she used before pregnancy. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Restart the combined pill from 3 weeks
Restart the combined pill today as before
Offer a progestogen-only method to start now
C.why: She is breastfeeding, so combined methods usually wait until at least 6 weeks. Progestogen-only methods can start immediately and cover her from 3 weeks when fertility returns.

whyNot.0: Three weeks applies to women who are not breastfeeding.
whyNot.1: Combined methods are not started immediately after birth.
whyNot.3: Mixed feeding fails the LAM criteria, so breastfeeding is not reliable contraception.

C.q: Ana, 1 day after a vaginal birth, would like an IUD and asks when it can be fitted. Which answer is most accurate?
options: Within 48 hours of birth, or else from 4 weeks
At the 6–8 week postnatal check with the GP
From 3 weeks, when her fertility may return
After her first period following the birth
C.why: NHS: an IUD or IUS can be fitted within 48 hours of birth; otherwise wait until 4 weeks after the birth.

whyNot.1: She does not need to wait until the postnatal check.
whyNot.2: Three weeks is when fertility may return, not an IUD fitting window.
whyNot.3: Fitting is timed by weeks since birth, not by periods.

C.q: Before transfer to the health visitor, Tia, 22, mentions a new partner and says she is unsure about STIs and contraception. What is the best action?
options: Advise her to wait for the 6–8 week GP check
Give information about, and access to, sexual health services
Tell her the booking IDPS screen still covers her
Advise condoms until her periods return, then review
C.why: SPM 3.4: midwives offer information and access to sexual and reproductive health services, including STI testing and contraception. Fertility may return from 3 weeks.

whyNot.0: Waiting risks an unplanned pregnancy and untreated infection.
whyNot.2: Booking screening does not cover exposure from a new partner.
whyNot.3: Periods are not a guide to fertility, and STI concerns need addressing now.

reteach.title: Three, forty-eight, four, six
reteach.question: Can four numbers answer most postnatal contraception questions?

blocks.body: 3 weeks: fertility can return, and combined methods may start if she is not breastfeeding and has no clot risk. 48 hours: the window for an IUD or IUS after birth. 4 weeks: the next IUD or IUS window. 6 weeks: combined methods if breastfeeding, and diaphragm refitting. Progestogen-only methods and condoms can start any time.

blocks.text: LAM fails as soon as the baby has anything other than breast milk, the baby passes 6 months, or any bleeding returns.

explain.body: Pregnancy is possible from 3 weeks after birth. A gap of at least 12 months before the next pregnancy is usually advised.

test.q: Why should contraception be discussed before a woman leaves postnatal care?
options: Fertility can return from 3 weeks after birth
Ovulation returns after the first period
test.why: Fertility can return from 3 weeks, so women need a plan early.

whyNot.1: Breastfeeding protects only under strict LAM conditions.
whyNot.2: Ovulation comes before the first period.
whyNot.3: Several methods can start straight after birth.

explain.body: Implant, injection, POP and condoms can start straight after birth, breastfeeding or not. An IUD or IUS can be fitted within 48 hours, or from 4 weeks.

test.q: Which method can start straight after birth for a breastfeeding woman?
test.why: The implant can be started straight after birth, including when breastfeeding.

whyNot.0: The patch is a combined method, usually from 6 weeks if breastfeeding.
whyNot.1: The combined pill usually waits until 6 weeks if breastfeeding.
whyNot.3: The ring is a combined method, usually from 6 weeks if breastfeeding.

explain.body: Combined pill, ring or patch: from 3 weeks if not breastfeeding and no VTE risk factors; usually from at least 6 weeks if breastfeeding.

test.q: A breastfeeding woman wants the vaginal ring. When is it usually started?
test.why: Breastfeeding women are usually advised to wait at least 6 weeks before combined methods.

whyNot.0: Three weeks applies when not breastfeeding.
whyNot.2: Combined methods are not started immediately after birth.
whyNot.3: There is no need to wait 12 weeks.

explain.body: Breastfeeding works as contraception when the baby has breast milk only, is under 6 months and periods have not returned. Any change ends it.

test.q: Which change means a woman can no longer rely on LAM?
test.why: Giving anything other than breast milk, including solids, means LAM no longer applies.

whyNot.0: LAM can apply up to 6 months.
whyNot.1: Night feeds help maintain LAM; stopping them ends it.
whyNot.2: No bleeding is one of the LAM conditions.
